paper: A. S. Fraenkel, Aperiodic subtraction games, Electron. J. Combin. 18(2) (2011) #P19

claims.claim: The printed a_n, b_n (n = 0..23) are what recursions (1), (2) produce: a_n = mex{a_i, b_i : i < n}, b_n = 2a_n.
A and B are complementary: every n ≥ 1 is in exactly one of them.
claims.result: 11,184,811 terms of A and 5,592,406 of B below 16,777,216; 0 collisions

claims.claim: For Mark, P = B and N = A.
P-positions are exactly the dopey numbers (binary ends in an odd number of 0s), N-positions the vile ones.
The elements of A alternate in spite (a₁ odious, a₂ evil, …); the same holds for B.
The printed g(0..23) and W is a ternary word (g ≤ 2).
The 0s of W are dopey and alternate in spite.
Every odious 0 is preceded by 1 and followed by 2; every evil 0 is preceded by 2 and followed by 1.
All 1s of W are odious, all 2s evil, and both are vile.
Conversely every vile odious number has g = 1 and every vile evil number g = 2, so g is computed from the binary representation alone.
Between consecutive 0s only 010, 01210 (leading 0 evil) and 020, 02120 (leading 0 odious) occur.
At R(n) = 1^{2t−1}0 a subword 01210 or 02120 begins, at R(n) = 1^{2t}0 a subword 010 or 020; all four subwords appear infinitely often.
claims.result: 0 exceptions over 22 values of n; all four chains appear in [0, N/2) (4) and in [N/2, N) (4)

claims.claim: From 1000 the second player (Peter) wins, from 2000 the first (Nathan); 15 is an N-position and 15 → 14 wins.
The printed MiMark a_n, b_n (n = 0..23) are what recursion (1), (3) produces (b₀ = 1, b_n = 2a_n).
For MiMark (misère Mark), P = B and N = A with B from (3).
MiMark P-positions are the dopey numbers with the powers of 2 swapped: 2^{2k} in, 2^{2k+1} out.
claims.result: 0 exceptions; misère and normal play differ at only 24 positions below 16,777,216 (the powers of 2)

claims.claim: The printed UpMark a_n, b_n (n = 0..23) are what recursion (1), (4) produces (b₀ = 1, b_n = 2a_n − 1).
For UpMark, P = B and N = A with B from (4).
B consists of 1 and the numbers whose binary representation ends in 1 0^{2k} 1 (k ≥ 1) or in 1 0 1^k (k > 1).
claims.result: 2,097,153 exceptions, all P-positions it misses (2,097,153 of 5,592,406): 3 = 11, 7 = 111, 15 = 1111, 19 = 10011, 31 = 11111, 35 = 100011, … — every n ≡ 3 (mod 4) whose final run of 1s is not preceded by "10"

claims.claim: B consists of 1 and the numbers ending in 1 0^{2k} 1 (k ≥ 1) or in 1^k (k > 1) — the set B′ the proof actually works with.
claims.result: 0 exceptions in 1 ≤ n < 16,777,216: the theorem's "10 1^k" should read "1^k" (equivalently n ≡ 3 mod 4)

claims.claim: A consists of the even numbers and the numbers ending in 1 0^{2k−1} 1.
The members of B alternate in spite: b_{2n} odious, b_{2n−1} evil.
(i) If 2t−1 ∈ P then 2t+1 ∈ P iff their spites differ; (ii) the spites agree iff R(2t−1) ends in 0 1^{2k}, and then 2t+3 ∈ P.
claims.result: 0 exceptions over all odd pairs below 16,777,216 (5,592,405 with 2t−1 ∈ P)

claims.claim: For Mark-t (subtract 1..t−1 or go to ⌊n/t⌋), P = B with b_n = t·a_n, and P = the dopey numbers in base t.
The printed Mark-4 a_n, b_n (n = 0..23).
Mark-t is aperiodic (finite check: no period r ≤ 4,096 holds on [M/4, M)).
claims.result: t=2: worst first break 4096 after n0; t=3: worst first break 2642 after n0; t=4: worst first break 12288 after n0; t=5: worst first break 10799 after n0; t=6: worst first break 2264 after n0; t=7: worst first break 24671 after n0; t=8: worst first break 28672 after n0

claims.claim: Misère Mark-t for every t = 2..8: P = base-t dopey numbers with the powers of t swapped (t^{2k} in, t^{2k+1} out). §7 lists misère Mark-t as open.
claims.result: exceptions t=2: 0 (differs from normal play at 24), t=3: 0 (differs from normal play at 14), t=4: 0 (differs from normal play at 11), t=5: 0 (differs from normal play at 10), t=6: 0 (differs from normal play at 9), t=7: 0 (differs from normal play at 8), t=8: 0 (differs from normal play at 8)

claims.claim: In Mark-t (t = 2..8) every N-position has exactly one winning move: never both a subtraction and the division reach a P-position.
Mark-t: the P-density is exactly Σ_{j odd} (t−1)/t^{j+1} → 1/(t+1), and the Grundy values fill 0..t (each with frequency ≈ 1/(t+1)).

notes.title: Grundy values of Mark-t, t ≥ 3 (open in §7)
notes.result: For t = 2 the value of a vile n is its binary spite. t=3: not a function of the digit sum mod m for any m ≤ 2t+2; t=4: not a function of the digit sum mod m for any m ≤ 2t+2; t=5: not a function of the digit sum mod m for any m ≤ 2t+2. The g-function of Mark-t stays the paper's open problem.
